title: Three Common Sleep Habits Are Quietly Damaging Your Brain. A 23,000-Person Study Just Named Them.
excerpt: Sleeping too little, napping too often, and chronic insomnia were all linked to white matter lesions that precede Alzheimer's. For South Asians, the risk profile hits close to home.
body:
The alarm bells around sleep and brain health have been growing louder for years. Now, the largest study of its kind has identified three specific sleep behaviours that accelerate a type of brain damage directly tied to dementia — and every one of them is common in the South Asian diaspora.

Published in the journal *Alzheimer's & Dementia*, the study analysed brain scans and sleep questionnaires from more than 23,000 middle-aged and older adults. Researchers at the University of Arizona examined five sleep behaviours — duration, daytime napping, sleeplessness, unintentional daytime dozing, and snoring — and measured their association with white matter hyperintensities, areas of damage in the brain's wiring that are strongly linked to cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease.

Three behaviours stood out. Sleeping fewer than seven hours per night, taking frequent daytime naps, and experiencing chronic sleeplessness were each independently associated with greater white matter lesion volume. Snoring and unintentional dozing during the day, by contrast, did not show the same link.

"Sleep is one of those potentially modifiable risk factors," said Gene Alexander, the study's senior author and a professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Arizona. "If we can improve the quality of our sleep, it may help reduce the impacts of brain aging and maybe even lower the risk for dementias like Alzheimer's disease."

## What the Brain Scans Actually Show

White matter hyperintensities are small areas of damage visible on MRI scans. They appear as bright spots in the brain's white matter — the network of nerve fibres that connects different regions. As these lesions accumulate, they disrupt communication between brain areas, impairing memory, processing speed, and executive function.

Previous research has established that people with high white matter lesion volumes are significantly more likely to develop mild cognitive impairment or full dementia. The new study found that those experiencing chronic sleeplessness had a 40 per cent higher risk of cognitive impairment — equivalent to ageing the brain by 3.5 years.

Lead author Madeline Ally noted that the findings on daytime napping were particularly nuanced. "Short naps may also be helpful for alertness and cognition," she said. The questionnaire did not distinguish between a brief 20-minute rest and a prolonged two-hour sleep during the day, so future research will need to untangle whether duration and timing of naps matter.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

South Asians carry a disproportionate burden of Alzheimer's and vascular dementia. Studies have shown that people of South Asian descent develop dementia at younger ages and at higher rates than white populations in the UK and North America, driven in part by elevated rates of diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease — all conditions that also damage white matter.

But the sleep dimension adds another layer of vulnerability. The diaspora lifestyle practically engineers the three risk behaviours this study identified. Late-night video calls with family in India push bedtimes past midnight. The pressure of long work hours in tech, medicine, and small business means chronic sleep restriction is normalised. And daytime napping — culturally ingrained and practically necessary after a short night — is the third leg of a vicious cycle.

Dr Samir Fahmy, director of the Sleep Disorder Center at NYC Health + Hospitals/Kings County, said the emphasis should shift from how to sleep better at night to how to structure the entire day. "Waking up at the same time every day, getting natural light exposure within the first hour, and getting exercise in the late afternoon or early evening" are the three anchors, he said.

Closer to bedtime, he recommends a structured wind-down routine lasting 30 to 60 minutes. "This may include dimming lights, avoiding blue-light-emitting screens, engaging in low-stimulation activities — reading, stretching, or mindfulness practices — and maintaining consistent pre-sleep cues."

## What Comes Next

The study's authors plan to follow participants longitudinally to determine whether improving sleep behaviours can slow or reverse white matter damage. They also intend to refine their napping data, distinguishing between occasional short naps and habitual long ones.

For now, the message is uncomfortably clear. The brain is keeping score of every short night, every restless hour, and every afternoon crash that stretches too long. South Asians in the diaspora — already facing higher baseline risk for dementia through metabolic and cardiovascular pathways — cannot afford to treat sleep as a luxury.

Seven to nine hours. Every night. No exceptions the brain will forget.

*Sources: Ally, M., et al. (2026). Associations of sleep behaviors with white matter hyperintensity volume in middle-aged to older adults. Alzheimer's & Dementia. DOI: 10.1002/alz.71457; New York Post; News-Medical.net*
